newsitem.title: UK: Gilts seen depressed by rate woes after budget.
newsitem.headline: Gilts seen depressed by rate woes after budget.

text.p: Prospects for British government debt were dimmed by Tuesday's budget as forecasts of an increase in consumer spending fuelled market concerns that interest rates would have to be raised, analysts said.
Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke, delivering the 1997/98 budget, said consumer spending would increase by three percent in 1996 and more than four percent in 1997.

"Clearly, with consumer spending at 4.25 percent then meeting that 2.5 percent forecast for inflation will require higher interest rates," said Paul Mortimer-Lee chief capital markets economist at Paribas in London.
"We are still looking for an interest rate hike before the next election," he said.
British base rates were raised to 6.00 percent from 5.75 percent on October 30.
December gilt futures were down 7/32 in automated trade by 1715 GMT. Before the budget speech, they were at 111-07.
Analysts said they were particularly concerned that inflation targets were over-optimistic. Underlying inflation was forecast to fall to 2.5 percent or lower.
The forecast for 1996 GDP was unchanged at 2.5 percent, while the 1997 forecast was upped to 3.50 percent from 3.25.
PSBR forecast was cut less than the market expected to 26.5 billion for 1996/97, but the 1997/98 forecast was cut by more than expected to 19.0 billion stg.

"He's right to predict strong growth next year and low inflation next year. But he's predicting too good a balance of growth," said Gerard Lyons, chief economist at DKB International in London. "He's too optimistic on investment and exports."
However, there may be some short term lift for the market as the budget appeared to be fiscally prudent, analysts said.
Overall, tax cuts were said to be worth 2.0 billion stg, against a Reuters survey predicting a net tax giveaway of 2.25 billion stg.

Kirit Shah, chief market strategist at Sanwa International in London, said the spread of 10-year gilt yields over comparable German Bunds was likely to narrow to 170 basis points over the short-term, from 180 basis points before the budget.

So far this year, the spread has had a roller-coaster ride. It ended 1995 around 150 basis points, before rising to more than 190 basis points in April. It fell again to the 150 region mid-year, before heading back to the 190s in November.
"There is nothing in this budget to shake the spread out of the 170 to 200 basis point range, with any narrowing short-lived" said Shah.
"But gilts still offer good relative value."
Mortimer-Lee said the spread would continue to hover around the 182 basis point level.
Shah said much of the good news for gilts in the budget had already been priced in, with gains earlier in the session pounced on by investors seeking to take profits.
December gilt futures earlier reached a high of 111-15, within striking range of the contract high of 111-17, set in October.

Analysts said the Bank of England would now be able to use Clarke's optimistic growth projections as an argument for higher interest rates, and that worry would prevent any further yield-spread narrowing.
"What Clarke has given with one hand he has taken away with the other," said Mortimer-Lee. "It's a neutral-looking budget, but it won't stop the Bank of England pushing for higher rates."
